t: Section 14(e) of the Voting Rights Act of 1965 (42 U.S.C. 1973l(e)) is amended by inserting “, reasonable expert fees, and other reasonable litigation expenses” after “reasonable attorney’s fee”.

fable.w: The tempting reading is that a litigation-related provision amounts to a right to sue the government. This amendment only widens the costs a prevailing party may recover in existing Voting Rights Act enforcement suits, adding expert fees and other litigation expenses. It grants no new right for an outside party to sue over or object to a federal decision, and it sets up no consultation, hearing, rulemaking, or advisory body.
fable.s: is amended by inserting “, reasonable expert fees, and other reasonable litigation expenses” after “reasonable attorney’s fee”

opus.w: This amendment only widens the fee-shifting provision so a winning party can recover expert fees and other litigation expenses. It doesn't give any outside party a new right to sue over, or object to, a federal decision, and it doesn't set up any consultation, hearing, or comment process. Describing how litigation works, as opposed to granting a right to challenge a federal decision, is not participation.
opus.s: is amended by inserting “, reasonable expert fees, and other reasonable litigation expenses” after “reasonable attorney’s fee”.
opus.b: 1. **Tempting reading:** The amendment deals with litigation. It adds expert fees and other litigation expenses to the attorney's fees that can be recovered in Voting Rights Act cases. That might look like it gives outside parties a way to challenge government action. It doesn't fit the definition, though. The amendment only changes which costs a winning party can recover. It doesn't create a right for an outside party to sue over, or formally object to, a federal decision. Suits under this Act are also mostly brought against state and local voting practices, not federal decisions. Changing the rules of litigation is a listed trap.

qwen_chat.w: This section amends the scope of recoverable litigation costs (attorney's fees, expert fees) in voting rights cases. It does not establish a new right to sue, nor does it require consultation, public comment, or advisory committees. The definition excludes procedural aspects of litigation such as jurisdiction or fee structures from being considered 'participation.'
qwen_chat.s: Section 14(e) of the Voting Rights Act of 1965 (42 U.S.C. 1973l(e)) is amended by inserting “, reasonable expert fees, and other reasonable litigation expenses” after “reasonable attorney’s fee”.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that granting the right to sue (via attorney's fees) constitutes "participation" because the definition states, "It does include the ability to sue the government over a decision." However, this section amends the Voting Rights Act, which typically allows private citizens to sue other private parties (like candidates or political committees) or local governments for voting rights violations, not necessarily the federal government. More importantly, the definition explicitly excludes "a court's jurisdiction, venue, or the statute-of-limitations period for suits - limiting or describing litigation is not the same as GRANTING an outside party a right to sue a decision." This text merely expands the scope of recoverable costs (fees) in existing litigation; it does not create a new substantive right to sue or a new participatory mechanism like a hearing or advisory board. It is a procedural amendment to litigation costs, not a participation requirement.
